identity.sample_label: 0.02Nb steel aged at 773 K for 3 h

summary: Fe-12Mn-9Al-3Cr-1.4C-0.02Nb (wt%) medium-Mn low-density steel strip prepared by near-rapid centrifugal casting and subsequently aged at 773 K for 3 h in vacuum. It is the lower-Nb reference of a 0.02/0.04 wt% Nb pair used to study how Nb microalloying and aging regulate nano-scale κ-carbide/NbC precipitation, austenite grain refinement, and the resulting strength–ductility balance.
composition: Nominal composition Fe-12Mn-9Al-3Cr-1.4C with 0.02 wt% Nb addition; measured composition 12.80 Mn, 9.01 Al, 3.01 Cr, 1.39 C, 0.021 Nb, Fe balance (wt%). Fe is the matrix element. Mn (medium-Mn level) and C help retain/stabilize austenite; Al lowers density and, together with C, enables nano-scale κ-carbide (Fe3AlC-type) precipitation in austenite; Cr is included for phase/corrosion control; Nb is the deliberate microalloying element intended to form NbC particles for austenite grain refinement. EPMA of the austenite matrix of the 0.02Nb steel reports Mn 13.12, Al 8.35, Cr 4.06, C 1.39, Nb 0.019, Fe 63.79 wt%.
processing: The ingot was prepared by induction melting in a water-cooled copper crucible, then re-melted and swiftly poured into a rotating copper mold to undergo near-rapid solidification into 60 × 70 × 2.5 mm strips. A portion of the as-cast strip was subsequently aged in a tubular vacuum furnace at 773 K for 3 h. This sample corresponds to the 773 K/3 h aging condition of the 0.02Nb steel.
microstructure: The sample consists of only two phases detectable by XRD: an FCC austenite matrix and BCC ferrite. At 773 K/3 h the ferrite content is 17.1 vol%, appearing as irregular-shaped islands randomly dispersed in the austenite matrix (as-cast ferrite content ≈16.2 vol%; aging at 723 and 823 K gives 16.4 and 18.3 vol%, respectively). The austenite contains a large amount of nano-scale intragranular κ-carbides coherent with austenite (orientation relationship [100]γ // [100]κ) and sparse submicron NbC particles with [100]γ // [100]NbC. As-cast 0.02Nb austenite grain size is 18 μm and ferrite grain size 3.6 μm; the austenite grain size remains almost unchanged after aging (no 773 K-specific grain-size value reported). XRD line-profile analysis for the 773 K/3 h condition gives an austenite dislocation density of 4.44 × 10^13 m^-2 (microstrain ε = 0.06) and a ferrite dislocation density of 9.55 × 10^14 m^-2 (ε = 0.258). Aging temperature and Nb content do not measurably change the phase constitution.
properties: At ambient temperature and strain rate 2.5 × 10^-4 s^-1 (gauge width 4 mm, gauge length 12 mm, minimum four repetitions), the sample exhibits yield strength 975 ± 18 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 1057 ± 21 MPa, and total elongation 17 ± 3%; the average Vickers microhardness is 455 HV (200 gf, 20 s). The engineering stress–strain curve plateaus near 1000–1050 MPa and terminates near 17–18% strain. Characterization performed includes: XRD (D/max-2500, 40 kV, 2θ 30–100°, 4°/min) for phase identification and dislocation-density line-profile analysis; SEM with EBSD (Apollo 300 thermal field emission SEM, 300 nm step) for ferrite fraction/morphology; TEM (JEOL JEM-2100, 200 kV) with SAED and EDS for NbC and κ-carbide identification; Vickers microhardness (MH-5L); and tensile testing (MTS Criterion 44).
mechanisms: 773 K/3 h aging promotes extensive intragranular κ-carbide precipitation in austenite; for this 0.02Nb sample the calculated κ-carbide precipitation strengthening is 230.0 MPa, exceeding the austenite dislocation strengthening (70.8 MPa) and becoming the dominant strengthening factor at aging temperatures ≥773 K.

The nano-scale κ-carbides are coherent with austenite ([100]γ // [100]κ) and small enough to be sheared by dislocations during plastic deformation, so they provide precipitation strengthening through an order/antiphase-boundary shearing mechanism rather than Orowan looping.

Aging lowers the austenite dislocation density (4.44 × 10^13 m^-2, ε = 0.06 at 773 K/3 h), reducing dislocation strengthening to 70.8 MPa; the concurrent rise in κ-carbide precipitation strengthening (230.0 MPa) more than compensates, producing a net increase in yield strength to 975 MPa.

Austenite grain-boundary strengthening remains nearly constant with aging (89.9 MPa at 773 K/3 h, Hall–Petch with kγ = 14.55 MPa·mm^-1/2), consistent with the essentially unchanged 18 μm austenite grain size.

Submicron NbC particles act as strong, dislocation-impermeable obstacles; because they are coarse, their Orowan looping contribution is small (4.2 MPa) in this low-Nb sample, so NbC contributes little direct strength and mainly influences grain-boundary pinning.

The ferrite contributes dislocation strengthening of 83.5 MPa (ρ = 9.55 × 10^14 m^-2, ε = 0.258); since Nb content and aging have limited effect on ferrite solid-solution and grain-boundary strengthening, the ferrite strength contribution changes little.

DFT formation-energy calculations indicate that Nb doping strongly raises the κ-carbide formation energy (Fe24Al8C8: 0.891 eV → Fe23NbAl8C8: 2.826 eV; Fe24Al7NbC8: 1.453 eV), so the low 0.02 wt% Nb level in this sample allows relatively easier nucleation and growth of κ-carbides compared with the higher-Nb variant.
conclusions: For the 0.02Nb steel aged at 773 K for 3 h, the trade-off between reduced dislocation strengthening and enhanced κ-carbide precipitation strengthening yields yield strength 975 ± 18 MPa, tensile strength 1057 ± 21 MPa, total elongation 17 ± 3%, and microhardness 455 HV. Compared with the 0.04Nb steel under the same 773 K/3 h aging (YS 1014 ± 16 MPa, UTS 1122 ± 14 MPa, TE 14 ± 2%, 465 HV), this 0.02Nb sample has lower strength but higher ductility: its κ-carbide precipitation strengthening is stronger (230.0 vs 156.8 MPa), while its grain-boundary (89.9 vs 125.8 MPa) and dislocation (70.8 vs 106.1 MPa) contributions are weaker, reflecting the coarser 18 μm austenite grain and lower austenite dislocation density. At 773 K, κ-carbide precipitation has become the principal strengthening mechanism in this steel.
